transcript:
Meeting: Aurelia Health - pilot throughput tuning weekly sync
Date/Time: 2026-08-06 14:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Reynolds (Redwood AE), Carlos Vega (Redwood SE), Priya Singh (Aurelia Lead ML Eng), Mark Devereux (Aurelia CTO), Lina Park (Aurelia SRE)

Summary: quick run-through of last 72h pilot results, tuned continuous batching and concurrency, discussed queueing highs during spikes, agreed to run a longer steady-state test and share cost implications.
Topics: continuous batching adjustments, concurrency targets, inflight queueing/backpressure, KV cache hit rates, fallback policy to smaller quantized model under burst, pilot pricing/burst options.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining, um we got about 45 minutes so we can run through the last set of numbers and the tuning notes, I believe Carlos pushed a few retunes yesterday right?
[00:18] Carlos: yeah, hi hi, thanks. We bumped the continuous batching window from 25ms to 35ms for the medium traffic slice, and we lowered the target concurrency to 24 for the large requests group. That reduced queued tokens but slightly increased p50 on short requests, kinda tradeoff.
[00:40] Priya: okay quick question, when you say 24 for concurrency, that's per-GPU or per-pool? We run a 4-GPU pool for the pilot.
[00:52] Carlos: good call, that's per serving-worker instance — so effectively per-GPU in your dedicated pool config. We set worker_concurrency=24 which is tuned for your payloads.
[01:10] Mark: we saw the dashboard spike last night where tail latency jumped to 1.7s, was that the same window you were testing?
[01:18] Carlos: yes, that was a burst event. The queue depth jumped because of a traffic fan-out from your frontend retries. There was simultaneous long-context requests which held KV cache and reduced effective batching.
[01:36] Lina: I think our frontend did an aggressive retry on 502s, so that multiplied the concurrency briefly. We have the trace IDs if you want them.
[01:45] Carlos: please share, that will help correlate. Also note the KV cache hit rate dropped to 62% during that event — so more work per request.
[02:00] Priya: 62% seems low compared to our baseline. Any quick wins to improve hit rates?
[02:07] Carlos: two things — prefix caching tuning and request shaping. For prefix caching we can increase the cache window and also enable stronger sticky routing so that conversational sessions hit the same worker which retains the KV state. For request shaping, adding a short client-side debounce reduces microbursts.
[02:28] Maya: to add, Redwood's routing supports session affinity and we can suggest a rule set for your API gateway. We'll put a short runbook in the doc.
[02:37] Mark: cool. On the cost side, how does raising the batching window to 35ms affect unit cost?
[02:45] Carlos: net effect in our tests was about 7% cost savings per token at 350ms avg sequence lengths, but short requests saw a p50 regression of ~30ms. So if most of your traffic is conversational multi-turn, it's a win. If you have lots of single-shot prompts, maybe lower window.
[03:06] Priya: our mix is about 65% short-turns (~64 tokens) and 35% long-turns (512 tokens), so curious what you recommend.
[03:16] Carlos: with that mix I'd suggest a hybrid: lower the batching window for the short-request route and keep the higher window for long-turn route. We can steer by endpoint or by request metadata.
[03:30] Lina: is that per-route config supported in the pilot environment?
[03:34] Maya: yes, we can do per-route policies — we've applied them for other customers. We'll show examples in the runbook.
[03:40] Mark: about fallback — you mentioned automatic fallback to a quantized variant during surges. How mature is that?
[03:47] Carlos: it's basically rule-driven today. We have a smaller quantized model family that is compatible and we've enabled automated fallback when queue depth or tail latency exceed thresholds. It's fairly mature but we recommend you run a regression check since outputs differ slightly.
[04:03] Priya: output quality is critical for us, so we need a safety net — can we flag and rerun critical requests?
[04:10] Carlos: yes, you can mark requests as high-priority and skip fallback, or mark low-priority to allow fallback. Also suggestion: rerun important requests asynchronously for verification.
[04:22] Maya: okay practical next step is longer steady-state test. Carlos, can you summarize the test shape you want?
[04:28] Carlos: we'll run a 20-minute steady-state at 80% of your projected peak with the hybrid window: short-route window 20ms, long-route window 35ms, worker_concurrency=24. We'll also enable sticky routing to boost KV hits. We'll capture p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens/sec, and KV hit rates.
[04:46] Priya: that sounds good. Also include a 5-minute high-burst spike in the middle to validate fallback and burst capacity, and we'll send the gateway retry patterns so you can replay.
[04:56] Carlos: perfect, that'll expose backpressure. We'll also capture queue depth histograms.
[05:03] Mark: on pricing — you mentioned pilot includes some burst capacity? We need numbers for finance.
[05:09] Maya: yes, for the pilot we include 2x burst for short windows, beyond that we have an add-on. I'll send the revised pricing sheet with explicit burst terms.
[05:18] Priya: can you also note how dedicated vs hosted would change the cost profile? We might consider private later.
[05:24] Carlos: hosted has more elastic routing but variable latency. Dedicated gives predictable throughput and better KV locality, so lower p99 in steady state; cost per hour is higher but unit token cost can be lower because fewer fallbacks and better cache.
[05:39] Lina: do we need to change our network setup for sticky routing?
[05:43] Carlos: just keep consistent client IPs and pass session-id header, nothing special in the VPC. If you go private on-prem there are additional network constraints but we can provide a checklist.
[05:56] Maya: small note on observability — we'll add per-route dashboards showing token breakdown and cost per token by model variant.
[06:05] Mark: great. Any surprises in the last run besides the KV dip?
[06:11] Carlos: we saw a small memory pressure on one worker that caused GC pause — likely due to a long-context request with attachment. We're throttling attachment sizes for the next run.
[06:21] Priya: yes we had a few long requests with embedded base64 attachments. We'll annotate the sample set to exclude them or treat separately.
[06:30] Maya: ok to summarize — immediate actions are the 20-minute steady-state test, runbook + routing examples, pricing update, and your sample prompt mix. Anything else?
[06:40] Priya: would like a short written note on expected regressions for fallback quality, so our product folks can review.
[06:46] Carlos: we'll add a short eval section in the doc with examples of differences and a suggestion for thresholding.
[06:53] Lina: I can coordinate the SRE deep dive for traces next week, prefer Thursday morning.
[06:58] Maya: we can aim for 2026-08-11 09:00 UTC, I'll send calendar invite once you confirm.
[07:06] Mark: thanks all.

Notes and rough timeline:
- 2026-08-07: Maya sends pricing + burst note (action)
- 2026-08-09: Carlos posts steady-state results and histograms (action)
- 2026-08-08: Priya shares prompt mix and annotated SLOs (action)
- 2026-08-11: SRE deep dive with traces (tentative)

References shared: pilot-runbook-v1 (link), burst-pricing-sheet.xlsx (link), replay-traces-0806.zip (link)

End of transcript.
